prompt: `pip install requests` into the system interpreter answers `error: externally-managed-environment`. What is that protecting?
hint: Who else imports from that interpreter?

choices.text: The package index itself, which rate-limits installs made outside an environment
choices.why: The refusal is local and happens before anything is downloaded.

choices.text: Disk space on `/usr`, which a distribution reserves for its own files
choices.why: The check is about ownership of the installation rather than about space.

choices.text: Programs that are part of the operating system and import from the same Python
choices.why: Package managers, printer configuration and firewall tools are written in it, and upgrading a library under them changes what they import.

choices.text: Your own project, which would otherwise get a version it did not ask for
choices.why: Your project is not installed into the system interpreter at all.

prompt: Two projects on one machine need different versions of the same library. Why does a single global installation not work?

choices.text: `pip` refuses to install a library that is already present at another version
choices.why: `--upgrade` replaces it without complaint, which is how this happens quietly.

choices.text: The two projects would share a `__pycache__`, which is keyed by version
choices.why: Bytecode caches sit beside the source and are not what this is about.

choices.text: It holds one version, so one project is broken and which depends on install order
choices.why: That is the whole problem an environment per project solves.

choices.text: Imports would be ambiguous, and Python raises at the point of the second import of it
choices.why: There is nothing ambiguous: one copy is installed and both projects get it.

prompt: What does a virtual environment isolate?
hint: One thing, and it is narrow.

choices.text: Which libraries the `import` statement is able to find, and nothing else
choices.why: It is not a sandbox: the filesystem, the network and the processes are the machine's, and that is the only thing this problem is about.

choices.text: The filesystem, so a script cannot read outside the project directory
choices.why: A script inside an environment reads anything the user can read.

choices.text: The interpreter, of which it holds its own compiled copy
choices.why: It holds a link to one; `pyvenv.cfg` names which.

choices.text: The network, so an install has to be approved before it reaches the index
choices.why: Installs go straight out as they always did.

prompt: When is `--break-system-packages` defensible?
hint: Something you are about to throw away.

choices.text: In a container you built yourself and are about to throw away at the end of the build
choices.why: On a machine you work on, an environment costs five seconds and this flag costs an afternoon later in the year.

choices.text: When the system package manager has no build of the library in question
choices.why: That is the usual reason people reach for it, and an environment answers it better.

choices.text: When you are the only user of the machine and have administrative rights
choices.why: Being able to do it is what the flag already assumes.

choices.text: When the library being installed is pure Python with no compiled parts
choices.why: Whether it compiles has nothing to do with whose installation it lands in.

prompt: The specification behind the `externally-managed-environment` refusal: `PEP ______`
What does `include-system-site-packages = false` in `pyvenv.cfg` do?
hint: It is the line that makes the isolation.

choices.text: It prevents the environment from being created inside a system directory
choices.why: The location of the directory is decided by the argument you gave.

choices.text: It keeps the machine's own libraries off this environment's `sys.path`
choices.why: With `--system-site-packages` it is `true`, which is occasionally what you want and never the default.

choices.text: It stops `pip` from installing into the system interpreter by mistake
choices.why: `pip` installs into whichever environment is active regardless of this line.

choices.text: It makes the environment copy the interpreter rather than link to it
choices.why: That is `--copies`, and it is a separate choice.

prompt: What is inside a virtual environment that is NOT there?

choices.text: A `site-packages` directory, which is created on the first install
choices.why: It is created with the environment, empty.

choices.text: A Python interpreter of its own
choices.why: `pyvenv.cfg` records `home` and `executable`, which name the interpreter it borrows.

choices.text: The activation scripts, which are generated by the shell on demand
choices.why: `bin/activate` and its variants are written at creation time.

choices.text: A copy of `pip`, which is downloaded when it is first used
choices.why: `pip` is installed into the environment as it is created.

prompt: A systemd unit runs a script from a project with a virtual environment. What does it invoke?
hint: There is no shell to run `activate`.

choices.text: `source .venv/bin/activate && python script.py`, as a single command string
choices.why: A unit runs a program rather than a shell unless one is asked for explicitly.

choices.text: `.venv/bin/python script.py`, directly, with no activation
choices.why: `activate` is a shell script, and a unit has no shell that ran it.

choices.text: `python -m venv .venv && python script.py` at each start
choices.why: Recreating the environment on every start reinstalls nothing and wastes the boot.

choices.text: `python script.py` with `VIRTUAL_ENV` set in the unit's environment
choices.why: The variable is a marker; what selects the interpreter is which one runs.

prompt: Why is `.venv/` in `.gitignore`?
hint: Think about what is inside it.

choices.text: Its contents change on every run, so every commit would carry a diff
choices.why: It is stable between installs; the objection is its size and its machine-specificity.

choices.text: Git cannot track symbolic links, and the environment is built from them
choices.why: Git tracks symbolic links; the objection is what the directory is.

choices.text: It is a build artefact — compiled extensions for one machine, absolute paths, a copy of every library
choices.why: It is reproduced in seconds from a text file, and committing it puts hundreds of megabytes into a history that can never lose them.

choices.text: It contains credentials, since `pip` caches index authentication inside it
choices.why: Index credentials live in `~/.pip` or in the environment, not in the directory.

prompt: Something about the environment is wrong and nobody can say what. What is the first thing to try?

choices.text: Delete the whole environment and rebuild it from the requirements file, in one command
choices.why: The answer to almost every 'it works on my machine' about dependencies.

choices.text: Recreate it with `--system-site-packages`, so a missing library is found anyway
choices.why: That removes the isolation to hide a symptom.

choices.text: Compare `pip list` against a colleague's and install the differences
choices.why: It works, by hand, and the rebuild does it in one command.

choices.text: `pip install --upgrade` on every package, to bring the environment to one state
choices.why: That produces a state nobody has tested rather than the one the file describes.

prompt: Why write `python -m pip install` rather than `pip install`?
hint: Which interpreter does each one install into?

choices.text: `python -m pip` installs into the `python` you just ran; `pip` is whichever script `PATH` found
choices.why: The failure it prevents is silent: the install reports success and the import fails, because the library went elsewhere.

choices.text: `python -m pip` resolves dependencies before downloading and `pip` does not
choices.why: They are the same program and resolve identically.

choices.text: `pip` is deprecated as a command and prints a warning on every run
choices.why: It is not deprecated and prints no such warning.

choices.text: `python -m pip` reads the project's configuration and a bare `pip` does not
choices.why: Both read the same configuration files.

prompt: You install one package and `pip list` shows five. What are the other four?

choices.text: Dependencies of the one you installed
choices.why: `pip show` names them under `Requires`, and `Required-by` being empty is how you know which package you chose.

choices.text: Build dependencies, kept so the package can be rebuilt without the network
choices.why: Build dependencies are discarded after the wheel is built.

choices.text: Optional extras, installed because the environment had no constraint file
choices.why: Extras are installed only when asked for by name in brackets.

choices.text: Packages every environment is created with, such as `pip` and `setuptools`
choices.why: Those are there too, and they are not the four in this list.

prompt: `python -m pip uninstall requests`. What is left behind?

choices.text: The `dist-info` directories, which record what was installed for later cleanup
choices.why: Those go with the package they describe.

choices.text: Nothing — `pip` removes a package and the dependencies only it needed
choices.why: That behaviour would need a dependency graph `pip` does not keep.

choices.text: `certifi`, `idna`, `charset-normalizer` and `urllib3` — all four of them, untouched
choices.why: `pip` has no concept of 'no longer needed', so an environment accumulates a layer of things nothing uses.

choices.text: Only the packages that something else in the environment also requires
choices.why: It makes no such check; it removes exactly what was named.

prompt: Which field of `pip show` answers 'is this something I asked for'?
hint: Look at the direction of the arrow.

choices.text: `Location`, which differs for a direct install and a transitive one
choices.why: Everything installed into the environment lands in the same directory.

choices.text: `Requires`, which is empty for a leaf package you installed directly
choices.why: `Requires` lists what it needs, and `requests` needs four things.

choices.text: `Required-by`, which stays empty for a package that you installed yourself
choices.why: `Requires` is the other direction: what this package needs.

choices.text: `Installer`, which records whether it was a person or a resolver that asked for it
choices.why: It records which tool performed the install, not who wanted it.

prompt: Why is there no `pip upgrade-everything`?
hint: Think about what such a command decides.

choices.text: Because the decision is yours — `pip list --outdated` reports, and you choose
choices.why: Upgrading everything at once produces a state nobody has tested and a failure with no single cause.

choices.text: Because `pip` cannot resolve a whole environment at once, only one request at a time
choices.why: It resolves whatever is requested, including a full requirements file.

choices.text: Because a package index does not expose the newest version of every package at once
choices.why: `pip list --outdated` asks it for exactly that.

choices.text: Because upgrading a transitive dependency would break the package above it
choices.why: Sometimes it would and often it would not; the objection is that it is a choice.

prompt: `requests~=2.31.0` and `requests~=2.31`. Do they mean the same thing?

choices.text: No — the last component is the one allowed to move, so one allows patches and the other allows minors
choices.why: In a fresh environment they resolved to 2.31.0 and 2.34.2.

choices.text: Yes — `~=` reads the major version and allows anything under the next one
choices.why: Then both would have given the same answer, and they did not.

choices.text: Yes — trailing zeros are dropped before the specifier is compared
choices.why: The number of components is exactly what changes the meaning.

choices.text: No — the shorter form is rejected, since `~=` requires three components
choices.why: It is accepted and means something different.

prompt: What does `>=2.26` allow that `~=2.26` does not?
hint: One of them has an upper bound.

choices.text: A version from a different index, which the compatible form restricts
choices.why: Neither form says anything about which index is used.

choices.text: Version 2.25 and below, when nothing newer satisfies the rest of the file
choices.why: Neither allows anything below 2.26.

choices.text: A pre-release, which the compatible-release form excludes by default
choices.why: Both exclude pre-releases unless `--pre` is passed.

choices.text: Version 3 and anything above it, which was allowed to break you
choices.why: `~=2.26` is the explicit `>=2.26,<3`, and writing it out is worth preferring because it cannot be misread.

prompt: `requests==2.31.0` is pinned exactly. How many packages are now pinned?
hint: Look at what `requests` itself asks for.

choices.text: Two — the package and whatever it declares an exact version of
choices.why: It declares no exact versions; its dependencies are all ranges.

choices.text: One
choices.why: It declares `urllib3 (<3, >=1.21.1)` and `certifi (>=2017.4.17)`, so those may be anything inside a range you did not choose.

choices.text: None, until the environment is rebuilt and the resolution recorded
choices.why: The pin applies at the next install, and it applies to one package.

choices.text: Five — the pin propagates to everything the package requires
choices.why: A pin applies to the package it names and nothing else.

prompt: What is a comma in `requests>=2.26,<3`?

choices.text: A separator between two packages on one line
choices.why: Two packages would be two lines, or two arguments.

choices.text: A preference order, tried left to right until something installs
choices.why: There is no preference order inside a specifier.

choices.text: An `and` — both have to hold
choices.why: It is the explicit form of `~=2.26`, and the explicitness is the argument for it.

choices.text: An `or` — either may hold, and `pip` prefers the first
choices.why: A specifier that could be satisfied two ways would be no constraint at all.

prompt: Pin so that only the patch component may move, in the shortest form: `requests______2.31.0`
Why is `pip freeze > requirements.txt` the wrong way to write one?
hint: Look at what the output contains.

choices.text: It lists everything installed, with nothing saying which packages the project asked for
choices.why: In a year nobody can tell whether `idna` is a dependency of the project or a leftover of something uninstalled.

choices.text: It writes the packages in alphabetical order, losing the install order
choices.why: Install order carries no information worth keeping.

choices.text: It omits packages installed with `--editable`, so a local package is missing
choices.why: It includes them, in a form naming the path.

choices.text: It pins to the version installed rather than to the one that was tested
choices.why: Those are the same version, which is the one thing it gets right.

prompt: A project removes a library. What does its `pip freeze` output do?

choices.text: It shrinks by one line, which is the library that was removed
choices.why: The four packages it brought in are still installed and still printed.

choices.text: It marks each orphaned package with a comment naming whatever had required it
choices.why: `freeze` writes no annotations at all.

choices.text: It stays unchanged until the environment is rebuilt from that same file again
choices.why: It reports the live environment on every run.

choices.text: It keeps printing the library's dependencies, so the file grows and never shrinks
choices.why: `pip uninstall` removes exactly what was named, and `freeze` reports what is there.

prompt: What belongs in `requirements-dev.txt` rather than `requirements.txt`?
hint: Think about what runs in production.

choices.text: `pytest` and `ruff`
choices.why: Installing them in production ships a test framework and a linter to a server that runs neither.

choices.text: The pinned versions of everything, leaving the main file as ranges
choices.why: The split is by what the code needs, not by how tightly anything is pinned.

choices.text: Anything imported only inside a `if TYPE_CHECKING:` block
choices.why: Those are needed by the checker and they are not what this split is for.

choices.text: The transitive dependencies, so the main file stays short and readable
choices.why: Transitive dependencies belong to a lock file, and they are needed in production.

prompt: The first line of `requirements-dev.txt`, pulling in the other file: `______ requirements.txt`
What should a hand-written requirements file carry that a frozen one cannot?

choices.text: The hashes of the downloaded files, which `freeze` omits
choices.why: Hashes come from a lock tool and could be added to either file.

choices.text: The exact versions, which `freeze` reports as ranges
choices.why: `freeze` reports exact versions; that is the one thing it is good at.

choices.text: A comment saying why a pin is where it is
choices.why: One line per direct dependency, with the version you tested against, and a reason where the pin is not obvious.

choices.text: The index the packages came from, which `freeze` does not record
choices.why: The index is configuration rather than a property of the requirement.

prompt: `requirements.txt` says `requests==2.31.0` and Thursday's install differs from Monday's. How?

choices.text: `pip` resolved the same requirement differently because its download cache had expired
choices.why: The cache changes speed rather than which version is chosen.

choices.text: A transitive dependency released a version inside the range `requests` declares
choices.why: `urllib3 (<3, >=1.21.1)` means `pip` takes whatever the index held at the moment you ran it.

choices.text: The build machine was running a newer Python, which changes which wheel is selected
choices.why: It would, and nothing about the machine changed between Monday and Thursday.

choices.text: The index served a different file under the same version number
choices.why: That is what `--require-hashes` guards against, and it is rare.

prompt: What is in a lock file that is not in a requirements file?
hint: It covers more than what you asked for.

choices.text: The packages the project asked for, with a reason beside each
choices.why: That is the input file, which a person edits.

choices.text: The index each package came from, so an install can be repeated offline
choices.why: The index is configuration; a lock file records versions.

choices.text: Every package, direct and transitive alike, pinned at one exact version, with its hash
choices.why: Usually with a hash of the file that was downloaded, and it is generated rather than edited.

choices.text: The order the packages have to be installed in, which the resolver worked out
choices.why: Install order is recomputed and is not recorded.

prompt: `pip-compile` annotates its output with `# via requests` and `# via -r requirements.in`. Why does that matter?
hint: Think about the objection to `pip freeze`.

choices.text: It marks which lines may be upgraded without recompiling the file
choices.why: Any change means recompiling, which is the point of the input file.

choices.text: It records the order the resolver visited the packages in, for debugging a conflict
choices.why: The annotation names the requirer rather than an order.

choices.text: It lets `pip-sync` uninstall the annotated packages first
choices.why: `pip-sync` makes the environment match the file and uses no annotation.

choices.text: It says which package is yours and which was dragged in, so a line can be deleted safely
choices.why: `pip freeze` cannot produce that, and it is the difference between a file a person can read and a list.

prompt: Both `requirements.in` and the generated `requirements.txt` are committed. What does the second one buy?

choices.text: Two machines install exactly the same code, transitive packages included
choices.why: And a pull request that changes the generated file without changing the input is a transitive upgrade, which is exactly the change you want to see.

choices.text: Protection against a package being removed from the index
choices.why: Neither file holds the package itself.

choices.text: A record of when each of the dependencies was added, which the input file loses
choices.why: Neither file records a date; that is what the history is for.

choices.text: A faster install, since the resolver has nothing left to work out
choices.why: It is faster, and that is a side effect rather than the reason to commit it.

prompt: What does `--require-hashes` stop?
hint: Think about bytes rather than version numbers.

choices.text: A dependency moving inside a range you did not choose
choices.why: The exact pins in the lock file do that; the hashes are about the bytes.

choices.text: A package being installed from an index the project did not configure
choices.why: That is `--index-url` and the trusted-host settings.

choices.text: A version being yanked from the index after you depended on it
choices.why: A yanked version is still installable when pinned exactly.

choices.text: A different file being served under the same version number
choices.why: With hashes in the file, `pip` refuses anything whose bytes do not match, which is worth turning on for anything that deploys.

prompt: `sys.path` inside an environment starts with `''`. What is that entry?
hint: It is a directory with no name.

choices.text: The directory the script is in, or the working directory in the REPL and for `-c`
choices.why: It comes before the standard library, which is why a file named after a module shadows it.

choices.text: An empty slot reserved for `PYTHONPATH`, filled when that variable is set
choices.why: `PYTHONPATH` entries are inserted as real paths.

choices.text: The environment's `site-packages`, abbreviated because it is the default
choices.why: That is spelled out in full, at the end of the list.

choices.text: The root of the filesystem, which is where absolute imports resolve from
choices.why: Imports do not resolve from the root.

prompt: A file called `json.py` sits in your project directory. What does `import json` get?

choices.text: Your file
choices.why: The error usually surfaces three imports away, inside a library that imported `json` and got yours.

choices.text: An `ImportError` naming the ambiguity between the two
choices.why: Nothing detects an ambiguity; the search stops at the first match.

choices.text: Whichever was modified most recently, since the bytecode cache decides
choices.why: The cache never chooses between two different files.

choices.text: The standard library, since the standard library is searched first
choices.why: The current directory is first, which is the whole of this section.

prompt: A library behaves like a different version from the one you installed. What are the first two lines to run?

choices.text: `print(lib.__version__, lib.__file__)`
choices.why: More often than not the file is somewhere unexpected — a user installation under `~/.local`, or the system's copy, because the environment was not active.

choices.text: `pip install --force-reinstall`, which settles it by replacing the copy
choices.why: That changes the environment without telling you which copy was being imported.

choices.text: `python -v` and a read of the import trace, which names every file tried
choices.why: It works and it is hundreds of lines where two would do.

choices.text: `pip list` and `pip check`, which report the environment's state
choices.why: They report what `pip` installed, which is not necessarily what the import found.

prompt: Which field of `pip show -f` do you compare against `__file__`?

choices.text: `Installer`, which records how the copy got there
choices.why: It says `pip`, which does not locate anything.

choices.text: `Files`, which lists every path the package installed
choices.why: Those are relative to `Location`, which is the one to compare.

choices.text: `Location`
choices.why: Comparing the two settles the argument in one line.

choices.text: `Requires`, which names the dependencies that might have shipped a copy
choices.why: A dependency does not ship a second copy of the package itself.

prompt: When is it worth deleting `__pycache__` by hand?
hint: Something that should be gone is not.

choices.text: When a `.py` file you deleted turns out to still be importable
choices.why: Its `.pyc` is still there, and it is the one case where the cache is visible day to day.

choices.text: After every `pip install`, so a stale compile cannot be reused
choices.why: The cache is keyed by the source and is invalidated when it changes.

choices.text: When switching between Python versions, since the cache is shared by them
choices.why: Cached files are named by interpreter version and coexist.

choices.text: Before committing, since the directory is otherwise tracked
choices.why: It belongs in `.gitignore` and is not tracked.

prompt: Predict the resolution: a fresh environment, `pip install requests~=2.31`. Which is installed?

choices.text: The newest release of any version, since `~=` has no upper bound
choices.why: It has one: the component before the last may not move.

choices.text: The newest 2.x, because the minor component is the last one written
choices.why: Measured: it resolved to 2.34.2, while `~=2.31.0` resolved to 2.31.0.

choices.text: The oldest release satisfying the specifier, which is the reproducible choice
choices.why: `pip` takes the newest thing that fits.

choices.text: Exactly 2.31.0, since `~=` pins what is written and allows only patches
choices.why: That is `~=2.31.0`, which has one component more.

prompt: `pip freeze` printed five lines for a project that installed one package. Which line belongs in `requirements.txt`?

choices.text: All five, since anything less makes the install unreproducible
choices.why: Reproducibility is a lock file's job, and the requirements file says what was asked for.

choices.text: The four transitive ones, since the direct one is implied by the code
choices.why: Nothing implies a dependency from the code; the file is how it is declared.

choices.text: The one the project installed
choices.why: The other four are transitive, and a lock file is where they belong.

choices.text: None — a requirements file holds ranges and `freeze` emits exact pins
choices.why: A requirements file may hold an exact pin, and often should.

prompt: Build an environment in the conventional place, from any directory: `python3 -m venv ______`
hint: Five characters, and the first is a dot.

prompt: An install succeeds and the import fails. The command was `pip install requests`. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The install needed `--upgrade`, and a stale copy was left in place
choices.why: A stale copy would import, at the wrong version.

choices.text: The package installed a namespace the import statement spelled differently
choices.why: `requests` is imported by the name it installs under.

choices.text: `pip` was a different environment's, so the library landed somewhere else
choices.why: `python -m pip` is the version that cannot be pointing somewhere else.

choices.text: The environment was created without `--system-site-packages`
choices.why: That would hide the machine's libraries, and nothing was installed there.

prompt: Which of these belongs in git?
hint: One of them is a fact and the rest are artefacts.

choices.text: `__pycache__/`, so the first import of each module is faster
choices.why: Bytecode is regenerated in milliseconds and is keyed to the interpreter.

choices.text: `.venv/`, so a new machine needs no install step at all
choices.why: It holds compiled extensions for one machine and hundreds of megabytes of copies.

choices.text: `~/.cache/pip`, so an offline machine can reinstall from it
choices.why: It is outside the project and is a cache of downloads.

choices.text: `requirements.txt`
choices.why: The directory and the caches are build artefacts; the text file is what reproduces them.

prompt: What does a lock file guarantee that a pinned `requirements.txt` does not?
hint: Count how deep the pins go.

choices.text: That the transitive dependencies are the same versions too
choices.why: A requirements file pins what you named; the packages those need are ranges you did not choose.

choices.text: That the packages come from the index the project configured
choices.why: The index is configuration and either file can be installed from any.

choices.text: That an install works with no network, since the files are recorded in it
choices.why: It records versions and hashes; the files still have to be fetched.

choices.text: That no package has been yanked since the file was written
choices.why: A yank is not detectable from the file.

prompt: A cron job runs a project's script. What is wrong with `source .venv/bin/activate && python script.py` in the crontab?
hint: Think about the shell cron gives you.

choices.text: `source` is a shell builtin that the shell cron starts does not necessarily have
choices.why: `.venv/bin/python script.py` needs no shell feature at all, which is why it is what a unit or a crontab should carry.

choices.text: `activate` cannot be sourced from a non-interactive shell
choices.why: It can; the problem is which shell cron starts and what builtin it has.

choices.text: The working directory is not the project, so the relative path fails
choices.why: That is a separate and real problem, fixed by an absolute path either way.

choices.text: `VIRTUAL_ENV` would be set for every later cron job on the machine
choices.why: Each job gets its own process and its own environment.

prompt: Which of these is NOT solved by a virtual environment?

choices.text: Two projects needing different versions of one library
choices.why: That is the problem it exists for.

choices.text: An install changing the version a system tool imports
choices.why: Nothing is installed into the system interpreter.

choices.text: A script reading a file it should not have access to
choices.why: An environment isolates which libraries `import` finds, and nothing else.

choices.text: A library upgrade in one project reaching another on the same machine
choices.why: Each project reads only its own `site-packages`.

prompt: `requirements.in` and `requirements.txt` are both committed. Somebody's pull request changes only the second. What happened?

choices.text: The file was regenerated on a machine with a different Python
choices.why: That happens and it would change more than one line, with a header to match.

choices.text: A package was removed and its dependencies left behind
choices.why: A removal is an edit to the input file.

choices.text: A transitive dependency was upgraded
choices.why: Which is exactly the change you want to be able to see in a review.

choices.text: A direct dependency was pinned more tightly than before
choices.why: That is an edit to the input, which would appear in the diff.

prompt: An import behaves impossibly and nothing in the code explains it. What do you look for first?

choices.text: A circular import, which resolves to a module that is only half initialised
choices.why: That produces a specific `ImportError` that names the cycle.

choices.text: A file in the project directory named after a standard-library module
choices.why: `random.py`, `email.py`, `types.py`, `test.py`, `token.py` and `queue.py` are the ones people write by accident.

choices.text: A stale `.pyc` for a module whose source has changed since
choices.why: The cache is invalidated by the source's timestamp and size.

choices.text: A second environment that is active in another terminal
choices.why: An environment affects the process it started in.
